Source step. `Synthesize()` consumes the fuzzer-provided UTF-8/SSML buffer and materializes it into shared decoder state `p_decoder`. `SpeakNextClause()` later drives clause translation by pulling characters back out of this decoder.

`ReadClause()` seeds its clause-reading loop by fetching the next decoded codepoint from `p_decoder` through `GetC()`. `GetC()` itself returns `text_decoder_getc(p_decoder)` at line 174, so this is the decoder-to-clause handoff.

As the loop advances, `ReadClause()` writes each fetched character into `buf` and records its source position in `charix`, materializing the attacker-controlled clause text that `TranslateClause()` will later scan and tokenize.

While scanning `source` into `sbuf`, `TranslateClause()` turns unsupported non-alpha punctuation into spaces unless the character is in `tr->punct_within_word`. The default translator initializes `punct_within_word` to only apostrophe (`tr_languages.c:214,274`), so punctuation in the witness can split word boundaries before translation.

When a separator is reached, `TranslateClause()` finalizes the current token by appending a space in `sbuf` and recording that word's source offset and length in `words[]`. This preserves which attacker-controlled span from the clause buffer will later be treated as a word.

For the current clause iteration, `TranslateClause()` selects one tokenized attacker-controlled span as `word`. This pointer, not the raw original byte suffix, is what the downstream translation logic processes.

The first translation of the selected `word` produces a `phonSWITCH` directive instead of finishing in the base translator, and `TranslateWord2()` materializes the alternate-language string in `new_language`. This is the first attacker-derived state that makes the later translator lifetime bug possible.

`TranslateWord2()` selects or allocates global `translator2` for that alternate language. The ASan allocation stack ties the later-stale translator object back to this call path through `SetTranslator2 -> SelectTranslator -> NewTranslator`.

The same attacker-controlled word is retransmitted through `TranslateWord()` with `tr == translator2`. The outer translation now holds a live alias to the heap translator object selected in the previous step.

During this outer `TranslateRules(tr == translator2, ...)` call, a later non-alphabetic character in the same word has no matching pronunciation rule, so the normal-text fallback sends that character and the live `tr` alias into `LookupLetter()`.

Nested fallback step. `LookupLetter()` probes English for that character by reusing the same global `translator2` slot, even though the outer translation is still holding `tr == translator2`. The staged patch changes this nested fallback to `SetTranslator3("en")` instead.

Root-cause step. The nested English fallback enters `SetTranslator2()` while `translator2` still points at the outer alternate translator, and the different language request takes the delete branch. AddressSanitizer's free stack shows the free at line 1283; clearing `translator2` here invalidates the outer `tr` alias that `TranslateRules()` is still using.

After `LookupLetter()` returns, the outer `TranslateRules()` loop resumes on the same attacker-derived word and immediately reads through `tr`. Because the prior step already freed the translator object behind that alias, this dereference becomes the saved AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free READ of size 1.
